Cod and sprat in a power-law background

Do the two Allee mechanisms survive when the rest of the community is a fixed background?

Published

November 11, 2026

Code 
library(mizer)
library(ggplot2)
options(mizer_info_level = 0)
source("R/build_model.R")
source("R/combined_model.R")
source("R/background_model.R")

# Results of the scripts in background/
res <- readRDS("background/scan.rds")

    ifelse(x < alive, "dies out",
           ifelse(x > 1e3, "> 1000×", sprintf("%.2f×", x)))
}
#' "min–max" of x with a fixed number of decimals

#' The scan result at one grid point
at <- function(phi_prey, phi_larv, cod_resource) {
    scan[abs(scan$phi_prey - phi_prey) < 1e-9 &
             abs(scan$phi_larv - phi_larv) < 1e-9 &
             scan$cod_resource == cod_resource, ]
}
variant_label <- function(cod_resource) {
    factor(ifelse(cod_resource, "Cod larvae eat plankton",
                  "Cod larvae eat background food only"),
           levels = c("Cod larvae eat background food only",
                      "Cod larvae eat plankton"))
}
scan$variant <- variant_label(scan$cod_resource)

# What happens at each point of the scan
#   barrier    a rare cod cannot invade the cod-free state
#   unstable   the coexistence state has an eigenvalue with a positive real
#              part (well above rounding error)
# and, where it is unstable, what is left 1000 years after cod are started
# 20 % above it
scan$barrier <- scan$R0 < 0.999
scan$unstable <- scan$lead_re > 1e-6
alive <- 1e-3
regimes <- c("No barrier: cod invade",
             "Barrier. Coexistence state stable",
             "Barrier. Threshold: both species persist above it",
             "Barrier. Threshold: cod take over above it",
             "Barrier. Cod die out from above and below")
scan$regime <- factor(regimes[with(scan, ifelse(
    !barrier, 1, ifelse(
        !unstable, 2, ifelse(
            above_cod < alive, 5, ifelse(above_sprat < alive, 4, 3)))))],
    levels = regimes)
n_regime <- function(k, cod_resource) {
    sum(scan$regime == regimes[k] & scan$cod_resource == cod_resource)
}
# The links that are switched on
on <- scan[scan$phi_prey > 0, ]

1 Summary

The combined model showed two mechanisms that can keep a collapsed cod stock from recovering: the emergent Allee effect of Van Leeuwen et al. (2008), in which a rare cod finds too little sprat to eat, and cultivation–depensation (Walters and Kitchell 2001), in which abundant sprat eat cod eggs and larvae. In that model cod, sprat and plankton are the whole community.

Here the two species are embedded in a fixed power-law background. In the coexistence state every fish meets food and dies at power-law rates, as in a community with a Sheldon spectrum. Only part of those rates comes from the other species and from the plankton. The rest does not respond to anything. Two parameters, phi_prey and phi_larv, set how much of the power-law rates the two predation links account for, from none (0) to as much as they can (1).

The main results:

  • Cultivation–depensation persists. Sprat predation on cod larvae lowers the invasion fitness \(R_0\) of cod in the cod-free state by a factor of up to 28. On its own it stops cod invading from a phi_larv of about 0.05–0.23, as long as cod eat enough sprat to hold them down.
  • The mechanism of Van Leeuwen et al. does not. Sprat as food raise \(R_0\) in the cod-free state, by a factor of up to 2.2. In a power-law background, cod depend on sprat only at 30 g to 1 kg, when they eat adult sprat, and there are more adult sprat without cod.
  • Competition for plankton takes its place. If cod larvae eat plankton, the more numerous sprat leave them less. That lowers \(R_0\) by a factor of up to 3.2 and stops cod invading at every point of the scan, even without larval predation.
  • The coexistence state is rarely the cod state. The background feeds cod whatever their number, so cod lose the density dependence that made the cod state stable. Over most of the scan the power-law state is unstable: it is the Allee threshold itself. Cod started below it die out. Cod started above it settle at a state with fewer sprat, take over completely, or overshoot and die out too.
  • The cod states are fragile. Where the coexistence state is stable, a cod fishing mortality of 0.002/yr is enough to collapse it. A cod state above the threshold collapses between 0.025 and 0.05/yr. The combined model’s cod state persisted up to 0.27/yr. Cod do not return when fishing stops.
  • Dilution weakens the barriers smoothly. With both links at half strength, \(R_0\) is 0.72 without and 0.45 with competition. At a quarter it is 0.94 and 0.78.

2 The model

2.1 A fixed background

In the cod–sprat model and in the combined model, cod, sprat and plankton are the whole community. All sprat mortality above 0.01 g is cod predation or a constant, and cod above the diet-shift size eat sprat or starve. Real cod and sprat have many other predators and prey. Those soften every feedback between the two species.

Here the two species live in a community that is not modelled. In the coexistence state every individual

  • meets food at a rate proportional to \(w^n\), with \(n = 0.7\), and
  • dies at a rate proportional to \(w^{n-1}\),

as it would in a community with a Sheldon spectrum. Only part of that food and of that mortality comes from the modelled species and from the plankton. The rest is a fixed background: an external encounter rate and an external mortality that do not change when cod or sprat do.

2.2 Construction

new_background_params() in R/background_model.R builds the model with the allometric workflow of the mizerEcopath package:

  1. newAllometricParams() sets up cod and sprat without any interaction. Each species has a power-law encounter rate, chosen to give its age at maturity, and a power-law mortality, chosen so that the juvenile biomass density falls as \(w^{-0.2}\). There is no satiation and no metabolic loss. The species are in steady state, with the biomasses of the cod state of the cod–sprat model.
  2. setFeedingLevels() introduces satiation and metabolism: a feeding level of 0.6 and a critical feeding level of 0.2 at all sizes. It raises the encounter rate so that growth is unchanged. From here on the species respond to a change in food.
  3. makeInteracting() switches on two predation links: cod eat sprat, and sprat eat cod eggs and larvae. Whatever predation this creates is subtracted from the external encounter and the external mortality.
  4. setResourceInteraction() lets the species feed on a dynamic plankton resource, a power law up to 0.1 g. Feeding on plankton replaces as much of the external encounter as it can. The plankton is a semichemostat at half its carrying capacity.

Steps 2–4 move food and mortality from the background to the modelled world but do not change any rate. So the coexistence state is the same steady state for every strength of the links: with the links at half strength, growth and mortality differ from those at nearly full strength only by rounding error (a relative difference below \(10^{-13}\)). The combined model had to recalibrate erepro at every point to hold its cod state fixed. Here that comes for free.

Life histories are those of the earlier models (sprat to 15 g, cod to 10 kg, predator–prey mass ratios of 1000 and 30). Both species enter as 1 mg eggs, and there is no imposed stock–recruitment relation (R_max = Inf).

2.3 The two links

The strength of each link is a fraction φ of the largest strength for which the background stays non-negative:

  • phi_prey: cod eating sprat. At 1, the cod that depend most on sprat get all their food from sprat.
  • phi_larv: sprat eating cod eggs and larvae. At 1, the cod that sprat eat most die only from sprat predation.

At 0 a link is absent and its share stays in the background. φ is therefore a measure of how little the background dilutes a link.

Code 
share_data <- rbind(
    data.frame(panel = "Food of cod", w = w(p_max),
               share = shares$prey["Cod", ], what = "Sprat"),
    data.frame(panel = "Food of cod", w = w(p_max),
               share = shares$resource["Cod", ], what = "Plankton"),
    data.frame(panel = "Mortality", w = w(p_max),
               share = shares$predation["Cod", ],
               what = "Cod eaten by sprat"),
    data.frame(panel = "Mortality", w = w(p_max)[present["Sprat", ]],
               share = shares$predation["Sprat", present["Sprat", ]],
               what = "Sprat eaten by cod"))
share_data$what <- factor(share_data$what, levels = unique(share_data$what))
ggplot(share_data, aes(w, share, colour = what)) +
    geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
    facet_wrap(~panel) +
    scale_x_log10(breaks = 10^(-3:4),
                  labels = c("0.001", "0.01", "0.1", "1", "10", "100",
                             "1000", "10000")) +
    scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1), labels = scales::percent) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c("#2a78d6", "#1baf7a", "#eda100",
                                   "#eb6834"), name = NULL) +
    labs(x = "Body weight (g)", y = "Share of the power-law rate")

Figure 1 shows what the links can account for at most. The pattern follows from the shapes of the spectra. The abundance of one species falls as \(w^{-1.2}\) among its juveniles. The community that the power-law rates stand for falls as \(w^{-2.05}\). A species therefore matters to others mainly near its own largest sizes:

  • Sprat as food. Cod of about 200 g, which eat adult sprat, can get 96 % of their food from sprat. Cod of 1 g get 2 %, and cod of 0.1 g 0.3 %. The small sprat that small cod eat are a negligible part of the food at that size.
  • Cod as predators. Cod cause up to 74 % of the mortality of the largest sprat, but only 1 % of that of 0.1 g sprat.
  • Sprat as predators. Adult sprat can cause 96 % of the mortality of cod larvae of 0.02 g, and 35 % of that of eggs.
  • Plankton. Sprat get nearly all their food from plankton (85 % or more), which is what regulates them. Cod larvae up to 0.1 g can get 99.7 % of theirs from plankton, and then compete with sprat.

This already bears on the two mechanisms. Cultivation–depensation needs adult forage fish to eat the young of their predator, which the embedding allows at almost full strength. The mechanism of Van Leeuwen et al. (2008) needs juvenile cod to depend on small sprat, which it does not allow: in a power-law background the dependence of cod on sprat lies with cod of 30 g to 1 kg that eat adult sprat.

2.4 Cod larvae and plankton

setResourceInteraction() moves food from the background to the plankton for both species. Cod larvae then share their food with sprat. The combined model deliberately kept this competition out by giving cod larvae a fixed food. Both variants are studied here:

  • Cod larvae eat plankton (cod_resource = TRUE): the workflow as it stands.
  • Cod larvae eat background food only (cod_resource = FALSE): the plankton share of the cod diet is handed back to the background. This is the closer analogue of the combined model.

2.5 Numerics

The model uses mizer’s first-order upwind scheme without size diffusion, as the workflow produces it and as in the cod–sprat model, on 200 size classes (\(\Delta \ln w = 0.081\)). The combined model’s second-order scheme with size diffusion was not carried over: with diffusion, steadySingleSpecies() leaves an unbalanced diffusive flux out of the largest size class of each species. The combined model avoided that with a senescence mortality, which would break the power law.

Steady states other than the coexistence state are found by projection, with Euler steps of 0.1 yr. \(R_0\) comes from cod_R0() of the combined model, which solves the discretised transport equation and is exact for this scheme.

3 Telling the mechanisms apart

As in the combined model, the invasion fitness \(R_0\) of a rare cod in the cod-free state is decomposed by taking one thing from the cod-free state and the rest from the coexistence state, where \(R_0 = 1\):

  • Prey: the sprat that cod eat. This is the route of Van Leeuwen et al. (2008). It is below 1 if cod find less sprat to eat without cod.
  • Competition: the plankton that cod eat. It is below 1 if the more numerous sprat leave less plankton for cod larvae. This route is absent when cod larvae eat background food only.
  • Food: both together, that is the growth and reproduction of cod.
  • Larval predation: the mortality of cod. This is cultivation–depensation.
  • Interaction = \(R_0\) / (food × larval predation). It is below 1 if hungry cod linger at the sizes at which sprat eat them.

\(R_0 < 1\) means that cod cannot invade the cod-free state. In the combined model that implied two alternative stable states, because the cod state was stable. Here the coexistence state need not be stable, so its stability is checked separately: from the leading eigenvalue of getStability(), and by starting cod 20 % below and 20 % above it.

4 Results

4.1 The cod-free state

Removing cod takes away part of the mortality of sprat, mostly that of the adults (Figure 1). Sprat biomass then rises by a factor of 1.06–1.89, depending on phi_prey only. The plankton that sprat graze falls, and with it the feeding level of sprat.

Code 
spec <- cases$spectra[cases$spectra$what != "Sprat feeding level", ]
spec$point <- factor(spec$point, levels = pts$label)
ggplot(spec[spec$w >= 1e-6, ], aes(w, ratio, colour = point)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 1, colour = "grey45", linetype = "dashed") +
    geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
    facet_wrap(~what, scales = "free_x") +
    scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_log()) +
    scale_y_log10() +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c("#2a78d6", "#1baf7a", "#eda100",
                                   "#eb6834"), name = NULL) +
    labs(x = "Body weight (g)",
         y = "Abundance without cod /\nabundance in the coexistence state") +
    guides(colour = guide_legend(nrow = 2)) +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom")
Code 
spectra <- cases$spectra
#' A column of the spectra at point i, at the size nearest to w0
spec_at <- function(i, what, w0) {
    d <- spectra[spectra$point == pts$label[i] & spectra$what == what, ]
    d$ratio[which.min(abs(log(d$w / w0)))]
}

Two things in Figure 2 matter for what follows:

  • There are more sprat of every size. At the first point, with the strongest prey link, the largest sprat (14 g) are 6.1 times as abundant without cod, because cod no longer eat them. They lay more eggs, so the smallest sprat (1 mg) are 2 times as abundant. Sprat of 1 g are 1.1 times as abundant. No size that cod eat becomes scarcer. In the model of Van Leeuwen et al. (2008) it is the other way round: without cod, sprat produce fewer young.
  • Sprat do not become stunted. Their feeding level falls from 0.6 to 0.51 at 10 g, far above the critical feeding level of 0.2. The plankton sits at half its carrying capacity in the coexistence state, so it gives way only so far: it falls to 0.62 of its abundance at 0.01 g. In the cod–sprat model, adult sprat fed at 0.34 with cod and at 0.18–0.20, their starvation level, without.

4.2 The regime map

Code 
map <- scan
map$log_R0 <- pmin(pmax(log10(map$R0), -2), 0.5)
ggplot(map, aes(phi_prey, phi_larv)) +
    geom_raster(aes(fill = log_R0)) +
    # Without the prey link R0 is exactly 1, which is no boundary
    geom_contour(data = map[map$phi_prey > 0, ], aes(z = log_R0), breaks = 0,
                 colour = "black", linewidth = 0.9) +
    geom_point(aes(shape = regime), size = 2.2) +
    facet_wrap(~variant) +
    scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#2a78d6", mid = "white", high = "#eb6834",
                         midpoint = 0, limits = c(-2, 0.5),
                         breaks = c(-2, -1, 0, 0.5),
                         labels = c("≤ 0.01", "0.1", "1", "3"),
                         name = expression(R[0] ~ "of cod in the cod-free state")) +
    scale_shape_manual(values = c(1, 16, 17, 15, 4), name = NULL, drop = FALSE) +
    scale_x_continuous(expand = c(0, 0), breaks = seq(0, 0.96, by = 0.24)) +
    scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0, 0), breaks = seq(0, 0.96, by = 0.24)) +
    labs(x = "Cod eating sprat, φ_prey",
         y = "Sprat eating cod larvae, φ_larv") +
    guides(fill = guide_colourbar(order = 1),
           shape = guide_legend(order = 2, ncol = 1)) +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom", legend.box = "vertical",
          legend.key.width = unit(1.5, "cm"), panel.spacing = unit(1, "lines"))

Figure 3 shows the invasion fitness of cod in the cod-free state and, as symbols, what the coexistence state is. Every barrier needs phi_prey > 0: if cod do not hold sprat down, the cod-free state is the coexistence state without cod, and \(R_0 = 1\).

Can cod invade?

  • Cod larvae eat background food only (left). Without larval predation cod invade, the more easily the more sprat they eat (\(R_0\) up to 2.2). Larval predation closes the cod-free state from phi_larv ≈ 0.05–0.23. At the strongest links \(R_0\) is 0.079.
  • Cod larvae eat plankton (right). Cod cannot invade at any point with phi_prey > 0. Without larval predation \(R_0\) is 0.70–0.93, and at the strongest links 0.011.

What is the coexistence state?

  • A stable cod state (●) at 6 of the 58 points with a barrier on the left, and at 1 of 72 on the right. It needs a strong prey link and weak larval predation. Only there is this model bistable in the way the combined model was. Even then the basin can be small: at 2 of these points, cod started 20 % below the state die out.
  • The Allee threshold (▲, ■) at most points with a barrier. The state has one real positive eigenvalue, of up to 0.2/yr. Cod started 20 % below it die out. Cod started 20 % above it
    • settle at, or cycle around, a state with more cod and fewer sprat (▲);
    • or take over, and sprat die out (■). If cod larvae eat plankton, cod then settle at up to 220 times their biomass in the coexistence state, limited by the plankton. If not, nothing limits them and they grow without bound.
  • An unstable state that cod cannot hold from either side (×), at the strongest links. Cod started above it deplete the sprat they depend on, decline, and are then finished off by the recovering sprat.

Why is the coexistence state so often unstable? With R_max = Inf, cod are regulated only through what they do to sprat and plankton. More cod mean fewer sprat, and that has three effects on cod:

  • less sprat to eat, which stabilises;
  • fewer larvae eaten, which destabilises;
  • more plankton for cod larvae, which destabilises.

In the combined model cod had nothing but sprat to eat, so the first effect was strong. Here the background feeds cod whatever their number, and the first effect is strong only where phi_prey is large. The mechanisms that produce the Allee effect are the same ones that make the power-law state unstable.

Code 
knitr::kable(data.frame(

    Prey = sprintf("%.2f", sapply(pt, `[[`, "prey")),
    Competition = sprintf("%.2f", sapply(pt, `[[`, "competition")),
    `Larval predation` = sprintf("%.2f", sapply(pt, `[[`, "larval_predation")),
    R0 = sprintf("**%.2f**", sapply(pt, `[[`, "R0")),
    `Growth rate of the instability (1/yr)` = ifelse(
        sapply(pt, `[[`, "unstable"),
        sprintf("%.3f", sapply(pt, `[[`, "lead_re")), "stable"),
    `Cod from above` = biomass_text(sapply(pt, `[[`, "above_cod")),
    `Sprat from above` = biomass_text(sapply(pt, `[[`, "above_sprat")),
    check.names = FALSE), align = "lrrlrrrrrrr")

4.3 Decomposition

Code 
dec <- scan[scan$phi_prey %in% c(0.48, 0.96), ]
factors <- c(prey = "Prey (sprat as food)",
             competition = "Competition (plankton)",
             larval_predation = "Larval predation",
             R0 = "All together (R0)")
dec_long <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(factors), function(f) {
    data.frame(dec[c("phi_prey", "phi_larv", "variant")],
               factor = factors[[f]], value = dec[[f]])
}))
dec_long$factor <- factor(dec_long$factor, levels = factors)
dec_long$row <- paste("φ_prey =", dec_long$phi_prey)
# Without cod feeding on plankton there is no competition
dec_long <- dec_long[!(dec_long$factor == factors[["competition"]] &
                           dec_long$variant == levels(scan$variant)[1]), ]
ggplot(dec_long, aes(phi_larv, value, colour = factor)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 1, colour = "grey45", linetype = "dashed") +
    geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
    geom_point(size = 1.4) +
    facet_grid(row ~ variant) +
    scale_y_log10() +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c("#eb6834", "#1baf7a", "#2a78d6",
                                   "grey20"), name = NULL) +
    labs(x = "Sprat eating cod larvae, φ_larv",
         y = "R0 of a rare cod in the cod-free state") +
    guides(colour = guide_legend(nrow = 2))

The factors in Figure 4 behave very differently:

  • Prey is 1.01–2.21: above 1 everywhere. It depends on phi_prey only. A rare cod in the cod-free state finds more adult sprat and grows faster through the sizes of 30 g to 1 kg. As in the cultivation–depensation study, food works against depensation.
  • Competition is 0.31–0.92 when cod larvae eat plankton. It too depends on phi_prey only, through the number of sprat in the cod-free state.
  • Larval predation is 0.04–0.97. It needs both links: phi_larv for sprat to eat cod larvae, and phi_prey for there to be more sprat without cod.
  • Interaction is 0.43–1.00 with competition and 1 without. Cod larvae short of plankton grow slowly through the sizes at which sprat eat them, so competition and larval predation amplify each other. Sprat as prey do not interact with larval predation, because cod eat sprat only once they have outgrown it.

4.4 Introductions

         y = "Cod biomass / biomass in\nthe coexistence state")
Code 
intro_end <- intro[intro$time == max(intro$time), ]
outcome <- biomass_text(intro_end$cod)
outcomes <- sapply(intro_factors, function(f) {
    outcome[intro_end$factor == f][match(pts$label,
                                         intro_end$point[intro_end$factor == f])]
})
colnames(outcomes) <- paste0(100 * intro_factors, " %")
knitr::kable(data.frame(Point = pts$label, outcomes, check.names = FALSE),
             row.names = FALSE)

The introductions agree with the regime map (Figure 5, Table 2). At all four points, 1 % and 30 % of the coexistence abundance die out. An introduction at or above the coexistence abundance establishes at the first three points:

  • where the coexistence state is stable, cod settle there;
  • where it is the threshold, cod pass it and settle above it, with sprat at 0.34 of their coexistence biomass at the second point, and extinct at the third.

At the fourth point even three times the coexistence abundance dies out.

Note that these introductions go into the cod-free state, where sprat are more abundant than in the coexistence state. The coexistence abundance of cod is therefore not itself the threshold.

4.5 Fishing

Cod fishing uses the length-selective trawl of the earlier models, so \(F_\text{cod}\) is the fishing mortality on fully selected cod. Two cod states are followed, at the first two points of Table 1:

  • the coexistence state, where it is stable;
  • where it is the threshold, the state that cod reach from above it. That state has 1.6 times the cod and 0.34 times the sprat of the coexistence state, and no longer has power-law rates.

Each step projects the model until every biomass changes by less than \(10^{-5}\)/yr, starting from the state of the previous step. The downward sweep starts from the cod-free state, with cod topped up to \(10^{-6}\) of their coexistence abundance before each step.

Code 
# Draw only the branches of steady states, not the jumps between them: each
# sweep is split where cod move between the abundant state and the depleted
# one
settled <- fb[fb$converged, ]
settled$segment <- ave(as.numeric(settled$Cod > abundant),
                       paste(settled$case, settled$sweep),
                       FUN = function(a) cumsum(c(0, diff(a) != 0)))
long <- rbind(transform(settled, species = "Sprat", biomass = Sprat),
              transform(settled, species = "Cod", biomass = Cod))
long$species <- factor(long$species, levels = c("Sprat", "Cod"))
ggplot(long, aes(F_cod, biomass, colour = species)) +
    geom_line(aes(linetype = sweep,
                  group = interaction(species, sweep, segment)),
              linewidth = 0.9) +
    geom_point(data = long[long$sweep == fishing$sweeps[1], ], size = 1.2) +
    facet_wrap(~case, scales = "free_x") +
    scale_y_continuous(trans = scales::pseudo_log_trans(sigma = 1e-3),
                       breaks = c(0, 1e-3, 1e-2, 0.1, 1),
                       labels = c("0", "0.001", "0.01", "0.1", "1")) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = col_species) +
    labs(x = "Cod fishing mortality F_cod (1/yr)",
         y = "Equilibrium biomass relative to the\nunfished coexistence state (pseudo-log scale)",
         colour = NULL, linetype = NULL) +
    guides(colour = guide_legend(order = 1),
           linetype = guide_legend(order = 2)) +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom", legend.box = "vertical")

Both cod states are far more fragile than the cod state of the combined model, which persisted up to a fishing mortality of 0.27/yr (Figure 6):

  • The stable coexistence state persists at \(F_\text{cod}\) = 0.001/yr, with cod at 0.96 of their unfished biomass, and collapses at 0.002/yr. The state is only weakly damped: cod return to it at about 0.0064/yr. The little of their food that responds to them cannot make up for even a small extra mortality.
  • The cod state above the threshold persists at \(F_\text{cod}\) = 0.025/yr, with cod at 1.5 times their coexistence biomass, and collapses at 0.05/yr.
  • Cod do not return at any fishing mortality in either case, because a rare cod cannot invade the cod-free state (\(R_0\) = 0.62 and 0.45).
Code 
sprat_table <- data.frame(
    `Sprat fishing F (1/yr)` = sf1$F_sprat,
    a = sprintf("%.2f", sf1$R0),
    b = ifelse(sf1$cod < alive, "dies out", sprintf("%.2f", sf1$cod)),
    c = sprintf("%.2f", sf2$R0[match(sf1$F_sprat, sf2$F_sprat)]),
    d = ifelse(sf2$cod < alive, "dies out",
               sprintf("%.2f", sf2$cod))[match(sf1$F_sprat, sf2$F_sprat)],
    check.names = FALSE)
names(sprat_table)[2:5] <- c("R0, first point", "Cod, first point",
                             "R0, second point", "Cod, second point")
knitr::kable(sprat_table, align = "rrrrr")

Van Leeuwen et al. (2008) proposed thinning the sprat to let cod recover, and in the combined model a sprat fishery did open the way back. Here it cuts both ways (Table 3):

  • It thins the sprat that eat cod larvae, which raises \(R_0\) in the cod-free state at first.
  • It also takes the adult sprat that cod eat. At the first point, where cod depend most on sprat, \(R_0\) peaks at 0.99 and never reaches 1. At the second point it exceeds 1 at \(F\) = 0.5 and 1/yr, so there a sprat fishery lets cod invade.
  • It lowers cod in the cod state in both cases. At the first point cod die out at \(F\) = 0.5/yr.

4.6 Sensitivity

Code 
knitr::kable(data.frame(
    Variant = sens$variant,
    `Sprat without cod` = sprintf("%.2f×", sens$sprat_free),
    Prey = sprintf("%.2f", sens$prey),
    Competition = sprintf("%.2f", sens$competition),
    `Larval predation` = sprintf("%.2f", sens$larval_predation),
    R0 = sprintf("**%.2f**", sens$R0),
    `Growth rate of the instability (1/yr)` = sprintf("%.3f", sens$lead_re),
    `Cod from above, min` = biomass_text(sens$above_cod_min),
    `Cod from above, max` = biomass_text(sens$above_cod_max),
    check.names = FALSE), align = "lrrrrrrrr")

Table 4 varies what sets how strongly the species respond, at the second point of Table 1:

  • The barrier is robust. \(R_0\) stays between 0.3 and 0.45, and the prey factor stays above 1.
  • Plankton that gives way less (resource level 0.8) lets sprat increase more without cod. Larval predation then matters more and competition slightly less.
  • Sprat and cod closer to starvation (feeding level 0.4) strengthen competition, but strengthen the prey factor against it too. Sprat still do not become stunted.
  • What happens above the threshold is not robust. Cod settle, cycle (resource level 0.2) or die out (feeding level 0.8), depending on the variant.
  • The numerics do not matter much: 320 size classes instead of 200 change \(R_0\) by 0.09 %.

4.7 Density dependence in cod reproduction

Code 
bh <- cases$reproduction
bh$stable <- bh$lead_re < 1e-6
bh$barrier <- bh$R0 < 0.999

The instability comes from cod having no density dependence of their own. The mizerEcopath workflow normally ends by giving each species a Beverton–Holt stock–recruitment relation with a chosen reproduction level \(L\), the ratio of recruitment to its maximum. That was tried for cod at 16 points (phi_prey 0.48 and 0.96, phi_larv 0.24 and 0.72, with and without cod larvae eating plankton, \(L\) = 0.5 and 0.8). It does not restore the bistability of the combined model:

  • It stabilises the coexistence state at 7 of the 16 points.
  • It weakens the barrier. To keep the coexistence state a steady state, erepro rises by a factor \(1/(1-L)\), and with it \(R_0\) at low density. The cod-free state stays closed only where \(R_0\) was below \(1 - L\): at 6 of the 16 points.
  • Never both. At all 6 points with a barrier the coexistence state is still unstable, and at all 7 points where it is stable cod invade the cod-free state.

A stable coexistence state needs the density dependence at that state to outweigh the positive feedback there. A closed cod-free state needs the positive feedback, summed from no cod up to the coexistence abundance, to outweigh \(1/(1-L)\). Both hold only if the positive feedback is much stronger at low cod abundance than at the coexistence abundance. Here it is not.

5 Comparison with the combined model

Combined model This model
Community Cod, sprat, plankton The same, in a fixed power-law background
Cod state Held fixed by recalibrating erepro The same steady state for all link strengths, by construction
Sprat as food for cod Barrier (the mechanism of Van Leeuwen et al.) for early diet shifts Never a barrier: raises \(R_0\)
Sprat eating cod larvae Barrier Barrier, down to a factor 0.036
Competition for plankton Excluded Optional. A barrier when included
The two barriers together Amplify each other Larval predation and competition amplify each other. Sprat as food does not interact
Cod state Stable up to moderate larval predation Stable only at a strong prey link and weak larval predation. Otherwise the threshold
Numerics Second order, size diffusion First-order upwind

6 Caveats

  • The background is fixed. It feeds any number of cod and kills at an unchanging rate. That removes density dependence that a real community would supply, and is why cod can grow without bound above the threshold. A background that gave way under pressure would behave between this model and the combined model.
  • One number scales each link. The size pattern of each link (Figure 1) follows from the kernels and the spectra and is not a free choice. Small cod cannot be made to depend on small sprat without a kernel that changes with size.
  • One biomass ratio. The biomasses of cod and sprat are those of the cod–sprat model. Their ratio decides how much sprat mortality cod can account for when cod depend fully on sprat.
  • Sprat respond weakly to food. With a feeding level of 0.6, a critical level of 0.2 and plankton at half its capacity, sprat cannot become stunted. Table 4 varies these.
  • Stability.
    • getStability() returns a ladder of real eigenvalues between about \(-10^{-3}\)/yr and rounding error, from plankton sizes that no fish eats. They hide how strongly a stable state is damped, so only instability is read from the eigenvalues.
    • The fate of cod above the threshold comes from one projection, started with cod 20 % above the coexistence state and sprat unchanged, and judged after 1000 years. Cycles were not characterised.
  • Numerics. First-order upwind on 200 size classes, with its numerical diffusion. With 320 classes \(R_0\) at the second point of Table 1 changes by 0.09 %.
  • Internals. cod_R0() calls mizer internals and was written against mizer 3.4.0.9001. The results here were computed with mizer 3.4.0.9003 and mizerEcopath 0.4.0.

7 Possible next steps

  • A background that responds: for example a second, depletable resource that stands for the other prey of cod, with its own resource level.
  • A diet of cod that shifts with size, so that small cod can depend on small sprat and the mechanism of Van Leeuwen et al. (2008) gets a fair chance in a power-law community.
  • Sprat that are closer to starvation in the coexistence state (a lower feeding level for sprat only), so that they can become stunted.
  • The fishing thresholds across the regime map, and a sprat fishery as a way back from the cod-free state.

8 Reproducing this document

File Contents
R/background_model.R The model, the cod-free state, the stability measures and the decomposition of \(R_0\)
background/run_scan.R The scan over the two links; writes background/scan.rds
background/run_cases.R Spectra, introductions, sensitivity and density-dependent reproduction at single points; writes background/cases.rds
background/run_fishing.R The branches under cod fishing and the effect of a sprat fishery; writes background/fishing.rds
background_model.qmd This document; it reads the three results files 
OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1 OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 Rscript background/run_scan.R
OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1 OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 Rscript background/run_cases.R
OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1 OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 Rscript background/run_fishing.R
quarto render background_model.qmd

The scan takes about an hour on 8 cores, and the other two scripts about 15 and 5 minutes. The model needs the mizerEcopath package, which brings in mizerFromEcopath.

This document was rendered with mizer 3.4.0.9003, mizerEcopath 0.4.0 and R version 4.6.2 (2026-10-29).
